content:
Gout is a type of arthritis caused by a build-up of uric acid in the blood, which forms crystals in joints. It causes sudden attacks of severe pain, swelling and redness, often in the big toe. Attacks are treated with anti-inflammatory medicines. If you have repeated attacks, long-term medicine to lower uric acid, such as allopurinol, can prevent them and protect your joints.

Symptoms

  • sudden severe pain in a joint, often starting at night
  • the joint is hot, red, swollen and very tender, so even a bedsheet can hurt
  • most often the big toe, but also the ankle, foot, knee, wrist, fingers or elbow
  • attacks usually peak within a day and settle over one to two weeks

Over time, without treatment, attacks may become more frequent and affect more joints. Lumps of crystals called tophi can form under the skin.

Causes and risk factors

Uric acid is a waste product made when the body breaks down substances called purines. Gout happens when there is too much in the blood, either because the body makes too much or the kidneys do not remove enough. Risk factors include:

  • being male, or being a woman after menopause
  • family history
  • being overweight
  • high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease or kidney disease
  • drinking alcohol, especially beer and spirits
  • sugary drinks
  • eating a lot of red meat, offal or seafood
  • some medicines, such as water tablets (diuretics)

Diagnosis

Your GP can often diagnose gout from your symptoms and an examination. A blood test for uric acid (urate) is usually done, ideally a few weeks after an attack, as levels can be misleadingly normal during one. Sometimes fluid is taken from the joint to look for crystals, especially to rule out infection.

Treating an attack

NICE (NG219) recommends:

  • an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of steroids, depending on your health and other medicines
  • resting the joint and raising it
  • a cold pack wrapped in a towel
  • keeping the joint uncovered or using a bed cradle at night

Start treatment as soon as possible. Ask your GP about having medicine at home to start quickly at the first sign of an attack.

Long-term treatment

NICE recommends offering urate-lowering treatment to people who have repeated attacks, tophi, joint damage, kidney disease, or other risk factors. It can be started after a first attack. The usual first choice is allopurinol, with febuxostat as an alternative.

  • treatment usually starts at a low dose and is increased gradually
  • blood tests check uric acid until it reaches a target level
  • you may be given colchicine or an NSAID for the first few months, as attacks can briefly increase when starting treatment
  • treatment is usually lifelong. Do not stop during an attack.

Lifestyle changes

  • lose weight gradually if you are overweight
  • cut down on alcohol, especially beer
  • avoid sugary drinks
  • drink plenty of water
  • eat a balanced diet, limiting red meat, offal and shellfish
  • exercise regularly

Diet alone is rarely enough to control gout but can reduce attacks.

Gout and your heart and kidneys

Gout is linked with heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney disease. NICE recommends checking for these. Managing them improves your general health.

When it might not be gout

A hot, swollen joint can also be caused by infection (septic arthritis), which needs urgent treatment. Seek urgent help if you have a fever or feel unwell, or if this is your first attack and you are not sure what it is.

Questions to ask your GP

  • Should I start long-term treatment to lower my uric acid?
  • What is my target uric acid level, and how often will it be checked?
  • What should I take at the first sign of an attack?
  • Could any of my other medicines be making gout more likely?

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
